extracted.intended_audience: product managers, marketers, and brand/communications teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for product managers and marketers on evaluating and crafting advertising/storytelling around product launches, with emphasis on brand fit, emotional resonance, testing, and crisis response.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Message and the Emotion Did Not Match
rubrics_metrics.description: A good product story needs to feel right, not just sound right. Apple wanted to show the iPad Pro can replace many creative tools, but the ad felt like a machine destroying creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the emotional tone of an ad matches its stated message: if the message celebrates capability or empowerment, the visuals and emotion should feel celebratory (not destructive or cold). Test whether viewers interpret the intended sentiment; watch for unintended negative emotional inferences (e.g., 'we're replacing you' vs 'we're empowering you').

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Promise Consistency (Stay True to Brand Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple historically positions itself as supporting creators and putting the user first. The Crush ad 'broke Apple's promise to creators' by showing destruction instead of creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check ads against core brand promises (e.g., 'we help people create'). Ask whether the creative aligns with long‑term brand narratives and past campaigns (Think Different, Shot on iPhone). Avoid visuals or narratives that contradict what the brand stands for, as that risks betraying customer trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and Timing Sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple 'missed the global mood'—at a time of public anxiety about AI and machines replacing human creativity, showing a machine crushing creative tools felt tone-deaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess external context before launch: social anxieties, cultural debates, current news, and legal or political sensitivity (e.g., AI job fears). Even conceptually neutral ideas can be read badly if timing or broader discourse makes them sensitive. If context increases risk, reconsider or reframe the creative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-launch Story Testing (Test the Story, Not Just the Product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't only test product function—test how the story (ad, slogan, website) is perceived. Show creative to users and ask what they think it's trying to say and how it makes them feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run qualitative tests with representative users focused on interpretation and emotion. Use simple questions: 'What is this trying to say?' and 'How does this make you feel?'. Use feedback to catch misreadings or harmful emotional responses before public launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Check List for Rapid Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: When negative reactions occur, use a short checklist: Are a lot of people upset? Or is it just a few comments? Did we go against something our brand usually stands for? Are people already worried about this topic in the real world?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you answer 'yes' to two or more questions, treat the problem as significant and act quickly. This checklist helps triage whether backlash is a small noise or a real brand risk requiring decisive response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology Structure — 'Treat Apologies Like Products'
rubrics_metrics.description: A good apology should: Be fast; Be clear; Be honest. Apple apologized quickly, pulled the ad, and acknowledged the mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apologies with the same care as product features. Apologize promptly (don't wait), use unambiguous language ('We're sorry' not 'if you felt bad'), and acknowledge the failure while reaffirming core values. Consider the apology a productized response: plan channels, wording, and follow-up actions in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swift, Direct Crisis Response (Own It)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple's quick apology and removal of the ad signaled they understood the severity and helped contain damage—'They didn't double down. They didn't stay silent. They owned it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the brand is clearly at fault or widely perceived as such, respond swiftly, avoid defensive/ambiguous language, and take concrete corrective actions (e.g., pull the creative). Timeliness and decisiveness are central to rebuilding trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and Weigh Audience Reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The backlash was 'swift and brutal'—artists and creators (Apple's core customers) voiced strong objections, and public sentiment matters for brand trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor social reactions, especially from core user groups. Distinguish concentrated, influential criticism (e.g., creators, thought leaders) from isolated negativity. Use signal (who is upset), magnitude (how many), and tone to inform whether escalation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-first Messaging (Put the User Before the Product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Across Apple campaigns the message was: 'The user comes first, not the product' and 'We build products that help you share your ideas with the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame campaigns around user empowerment and creative outcomes rather than product dominance. Ads should demonstrate how people use the product to create, not show the product displacing or erasing human activity. Emphasize human stories and use-cases to maintain warmth and approachability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Emotional Trust (Feeling Matters as Much as Specs)
rubrics_metrics.description: People don't just buy because products work; they buy because 'the brand feels human, creative, and kind.' The Crush ad removed that feeling and damaged trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ads not only on features communicated but on the emotional associations they produce. Use qualitative metrics (sentiment, perceived warmth, empathy) in creative evaluation and consider downstream effects on brand trust.
